The lxx adds that he sat on a dunghill outside the city: the dunghill is taken from the passage <reference osisRef="Ps.113.7">Psa 113:7</reference>, and the ”outside the city” from the law of the מצרע. In addition to the four losses, a fifth temptation, in the form of a disease incurable in the eye of man, is now come upon Job: a natural disease, but brought on by Satan, permitted, and therefore decreed, by God. Satan does not appear again throughout the whole book. Evil has not only a personal existence in the invisible world, but also its agents and instruments in this; and by these it is henceforth manifested.
entries.e9fa85755204e1c2216dd77109bad6bf43da31fb: <reference osisRef="Job.2.9">Job 2:9</reference> <div eID="gen6916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6917" type="x-p"/> First Job’s Wife (who is only mentioned in one other passage (<reference osisRef="Job.19.17">Job 19:17</reference>), where Job complains that his breath is offensive to her) Comes to Him: 9  Then his wife said to him, Dost thou still hold fast thine integrity? renounce God, and die. <div eID="gen6917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6918" type="x-p"/> In the lxx the words of his wife are unskilfully extended. The few words as they stand are sufficiently characteristic. They are not to be explained, Call on God for the last time, and then die (von Gerl.); or, Call on Him that thou die (according to Ges. §130, 2); but בּרך signifies, as Job’s answer shows, to take leave of. She therefore counsels Job to do that which Satan has boasted to accomplish. And notwithstanding, Hengstenberg, in his <hi type="italic">Lecture on the Book of Job</hi> (1860),<note placement="foot">Clark’s Foreign Theological Library.</note> defends her against the too severe judgment of expositors. Her desperation, says he, proceeds from her strong love for her husband; and if she had to suffer the same herself, she would probably have struggled against despair. But love hopeth all things; love keeps its despondency hidden even when it desponds; love has no such godless utterance, as to say, Renounce God; and none so unloving, as to say, Die. No, indeed! this woman is truly <hi type="italic">diaboli adjutrix</hi> (August.); a tool of the temper (Ebrard); <hi type="italic">impiae carnis praeco</hi> (Brentius). And though Calvin goes too far when he calls her not only <hi type="italic">organum Satanae, </hi>but even <hi type="italic">Proserpinam et Furiam infernalem,</hi> the title of another Xantippe, against which Hengstenberg defends her, is indeed rather flattery than slander. Tobias’ Anna is her copy.<note placement="foot">She says to the blind Tobias, when she is obliged to work for the support of the family, and does not act straightforwardly towards him: ποῦ εἰσὶν αἱ ἐλεημοσύναι σου καὶ αἱ δικαιοσύναι σου, ἰδοὺ γνωστὰ πάντα μετὰ σοῦ, i.e., (as Sengelmann, <hi type="italic">Book of Tobit</hi>, 1857, and O. F. Fritzsche, <hi type="italic">Handbuch zu d. Apokr. Lief</hi>. ii. S. 36, correctly explain) one sees from thy misfortunes that thy virtue is not of much avail to thee. She appears still more like Job in the revised text: <hi type="italic">manifeste vana facta est spes tua et eleemosynae tuae modo apparuerunt</hi>, i.e., thy benevolence has obviously brought us to poverty. In the text of Jerome a parallel between Tobias and Job precedes this utterance of Tobias’ wife.</note> <div eID="gen6918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6919" type="x-p"/> What experience of life and insight the writer manifests in introducing Job’s wife as the mocking opposer of his constant piety! Job has lost his children, but this wife he has retained, for he needed not to be tried by losing her: he was proved sufficiently by having her. She is further on once referred to, but even then not to her advantage. Why, asks Chrysostom, did the devil leave him this wife? Because he thought her a good scourge, by which to plague him more acutely than by any other means. Moreover, the thought is not far distant, that God left her to him in order that when, in the glorious issue of his sufferings, he receives everything doubled, he might not have this thorn in the flesh also doubled.<note placement="foot">The delicate design of the writer here must not be overlooked: it has something of the tragi-comic about it, and has furnished acceptable material for epigrammatic writers not first from Kästner, but from early times (vid., <hi type="italic">das Epigramm vom J.</hi> 1696, in Serpilius’ <hi type="italic">Personalia Iobi</hi>). Vid., a Jewish proverb relating thereto in Tendlau, <hi type="italic">Sprüchw. u. Redensarten deutsch-jüd. Vorzeit</hi> (1860), S. 11.</note> <div eID="gen6919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6920" type="x-p"/> What enmity towards God, what uncharitableness towards her husband, is there in her sarcastic words, which, if they are more than mockery, counsel him to suicide! (Ebrard). But he repels them in a manner becoming himself.
entries.18363daad85bc68b94a8049fd1cc976d3c1a6696: <reference osisRef="Job.2.10">Job 2:10</reference> <reference osisRef="Job.2.10">10</reference>  But he said to her, As one of the ungodly would speak, thou speakest. Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not also receive evil? <div eID="gen6920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6921" type="x-p"/> The answer of Job is strong but not harsh, for the אחת (comp. <reference osisRef="2Sam.13.13">2Sa 13:13</reference>) is somewhat soothing. The translation “as one of the foolish women” does not correspond to the Hebrew; נבל is one wxo thinks madly and acts impiously. What follows is a double question, גּם for הגם. The גּם stands at the beginning of the sentence, but logically belongs to the second part, towards which pronunciation and reading must hurry over the first, - a frequent occurrence after interrogative particles, e.g., Num 16:22; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.5.4">Isa 5:4</reference></hi>; after causal particles, e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.12.1">Isa 12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.24">Pro 1:24</reference>; after the negative פּן, Deu 8:12., and often. Hupfeld renders the thought expressed in the double question very correctly: <hi type="italic">bonum quidem hucusque a Deo accepimus, malum vero jam non item accipiemus?</hi> גּם is found also elsewhere at the beginning of a sentence, although belonging to a later clause, and that indeed not always the one immediately following, e.g., Hos 6:11; Zec 9:11; the same syntax is to be found with אף, אך, and רק. קבּל, like תּמּה, is a word common to the book of Job and Proverbs (<reference osisRef="Prov.19.20">Pro 19:20</reference>); besides these, it is found only in books written after the exile, and is more Aramaic than Hebraic. By this answer which Job gives to his wife, he has repelled the sixth temptation. For 10b In all this Job sinned not with his lips. 10 <hi type="italic">b</hi>  In all this Job sinned not with his lips. <div eID="gen6921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6922" type="x-p"/> The Targum adds: but in his thoughts he already cherished sinful words. בּשׂפתיו is certainly not undesignedly introduced here and omitted in Job 1:22. The temptation to murmur was now already at work within him, but he was its master, so that no murmur escaped him.
entries.0840a04a5f7e286fb68cbcf1fa294f1192ce92ae: <reference osisRef="Job.2.11">Job 2:11</reference> <div eID="gen6922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6923" type="x-p"/> After the sixth temptation there comes a seventh; and now the real conflict begins, through which the hero of the book passes, not indeed without sinning, but still triumphantly. 11  When Job’s three friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place; Eliphaz from Teman, and Bildad from Shuach, and Zophar from Naama: for they had made an appointment to come together to go and sympathize with him, and comfort him. אליפז is, according to Gen 36, an old Idumaean name (transposed = <hi type="italic">Phasaël</hi> in the history of the Herodeans; according to Michaelis, <hi type="italic">Suppl</hi>. p. 87; <hi type="italic">cui Deus aurum est,</hi> comp. <reference osisRef="Job.22.25">Job 22:25</reference>), and תּימן a district of Idumaea, celebrated for its native wisdom (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.7">Jer 49:7</reference>; Bar. 3:22f.). But also in East-Hauran a <hi type="italic">Têmâ</hi> is still found (described by Wetzstein in his <hi type="italic">Bericht über seine Reise in den beiden Trachonen und um das Hauran-Gebirge, Zeitschr. für allg. Erdkunde,</hi> 1859), and about fifteen miles south of <hi type="italic">Têmâ</hi>, a <hi type="italic">Bûzân</hi> suggestive of Elihu’s surname (comp. <reference osisRef="Jer.25.23">Jer 25:23</reference>). שׁוּח we know only from Gen 25 as the son of Abraham and Keturah, who settled in the east country. Accordingly it must be a district of Arabia lying not very far from Idumaea: it might be compared with trans-Hauran <hi type="italic">Schakka</hi>, though the sound, however, of the word makes it scarcely admissible, which is undoubtedly one and the same with Dakkai'a, east from Batanaea, mentioned in Ptolem. v. 15. נעמה is a name frequent in Syria and Palestine: there is a town of the Jewish Shephêla (the low ground by the Mediterranean) of this name, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.41">Jos 15:41</reference>, which, however, can hardly be intended here. הבּאה is <hi type="italic">Milel</hi>, consequently third pers. with the art. instead of the relative pron. (as, besides here, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.21">Gen 18:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.46.27">Gen 46:27</reference>), vid., Ges. §109 <hi type="italic">ad init.</hi> The <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. נועד is strongly taken by some expositors as the same meaning with נועץ, to confer with, appoint a meeting: it signifies, to assemble themselves, to meet in an appointed place at an appointed time (<reference osisRef="Neh.6.2">Neh 6:2</reference>). Reports spread among the mounted tribes of the Arabian desert with the rapidity of telegraphic despatches.
entries.600342e80ec599fec697838dc08ec90d0e4caa9c: <reference osisRef="Job.2.12">Job 2:12</reference> <div eID="gen6923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6924" type="x-p"/> Their Arrival: 12  And when they lifted up their eyes afar off, and knew him not, they lifted up their voice, and wept; and they rent every one his mantle, and threw dust upon their heads toward heaven. <div eID="gen6924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6925" type="x-p"/> They saw a form which seemed to be Job, but in which they were not able to recognise him. Then they weep and rend their outer garments, and catch up dust to throw up towards heaven (<reference osisRef="1Sam.4.12">1Sa 4:12</reference>), that it may fall again upon their heads. The casting up of dust on high is the outwards sign of intense suffering, and, as von Gerlach rightly remarks, of that which causes him to cry to heaven.
entries.25a92c76a6dc738a239e7a4e881000564862e57c: <reference osisRef="Job.2.13">Job 2:13</reference> <div eID="gen6925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6926" type="x-p"/> Their Silence: 13  And they sat with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights; and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his pain was very great. <div eID="gen6926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6927" type="x-p"/> Ewald erroneously thinks that custom and propriety prescribed this seven days’ silence; it was (as <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.15">Eze 3:15</reference>) the force of the impression produced on them, and the fear of annoying the sufferer. But their long silence shows that they had not fully realized the purpose of their visit. Their feeling is overpowered by reflection, their sympathy by dismay. It is a pity that they let Job utter the first word, which they might have prevented by some word of kindly solace; for, becoming first fully conscious of the difference between his present and former position from their conduct, he breaks forth with curses.  <chapter eID="Job.2"/> <div eID="gen6927" type="x-p"/>

And this he did not with soft Linnen Cloaths, either because he had not now a sufficient quantity of them for so much use; or be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause therein he must have had the help of others who abhorred to come near him, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                        <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 13, 14, 15. Nor with his own Hands or Fingers which were also ulcerous, and so unfit for that use, and besides he loathed to touch himself; but with Potsherds, either be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause they were next at hand, and ready for his present use; or in token of his Repentance and deep Humiliation under Gods heavy hand, which made him decline all things which favoured of ten<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derness and delicacy,</ns0:note>] to scrape himself withal; and [he sat down among the ashes <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>In dust or ashes,</ns0:hi> as Mourners used to do: Of which see <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 42. 6. <ns0:hi>Ionah.</ns0:hi> 3. 6. <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 11. 21.</ns0:note>.]</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9. Then said [his Wife <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Whom the Devil spared with cruel intent to be the Instru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment of his Temptations, and the aggravation of <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi>'s misery by unnatural unkindness to him, which is declared <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 19. 17. and elsewhere.</ns0:note>] unto him, [Dost thou still retain thine Integrity <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Art thou yet so weak to persist in the practice of Pi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ety, when it is not only unprofitable to thee, but the chief occasi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on of all these thy insupportable miseries, and when God himself not only forsakes and leaves thee in this helpless and hopeless con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dition, but is turned to be thy greatest Enemy?</ns0:note>?] [<ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>bless.</ns0:hi> 1 Kin. 21. 10. 13.</ns0:note> curse God and die <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Seeing thy bles<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sing of God availeth thee so little, it is time to change thy note, <ns0:hi>Curse God and die, i. e.</ns0:hi> reproach him to his face, and tell him of his Injustice, and Unkindness to thee, and that he loves his Ene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mies, and hates his Friends, and that will provoke him to take away thy Life, and so end thy Torments. Or, curie God, though thou die for it: But although this word somtimes signifies <ns0:hi>cursing,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 1. 11. and 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 21. 10. yet most properly and generally it signifies <ns0:hi>blessing,</ns0:hi> and so it may very well be understood here as a Sarcastical or Ironical Expression, such as there are many in Scrip<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture, as <ns0:hi>Eccles.</ns0:hi> 11. 9. <ns0:hi>Lam.</ns0:hi> 4. 21. and in all Authors. And so the fence may be this, <ns0:hi>Bliss God and die; i. e.</ns0:hi> I see thou art set upon blessing of God, thou blessest God for giving, and thou blessest God for taking away, and thou art still blessing of God for thy loathsom and tormenting Diseases, and he rewards thee ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cordingly, giving thee more and more of that kind of Mercy for which thou blessest and praisest him. Go on therefore in this thy pious and generous course, and die as a Fool dieth, and carry this Reputation to thy Grave, that thou hadst not common sense in thee to discern between good and evil, between thy Friends and thy Foes. Or rather awake out of this stupidity and Lethargy, and give over this absurd and unreasonable practise, and as God gives thee no Help nor Comfort, let him lose thy Praises and Service. And this being her sense, it is not strange he reproveth her so sharply for it. And yet it seems hard to think that <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi>'s Wife should arrive at that height of Impudence and Impiety, as in plain terms to bid him, <ns0:hi>curse God.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>]</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10. But he said unto her, Thou speakest [as one of the foolish <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Like a rash, and inconsiderate, and weak person, that dost not understand, nor mind what thou sayest. Or, like a wicked and most prophane person; for such are frequently called <ns0:hi>Fools</ns0:hi> in Scripture, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 14. 1. and 74. 18. and every where in the Proverbs.</ns0:note>] Women speaketh: What! [Shall we receive good at the Hand of God, and shall we not re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceive evil? <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Shall we poor Worms give Laws to our Supream Lord and Governour, and oblige him always to bless and favour us, and never to afflict us? And shall not those great and manifold, and long-continued Mer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cies which from time to time God hath freely and graciously given us, compensate for these short afflictions? Ought we not to bless God for those Mercies which we did not deserve, and contentedly to bear those Corrections which we deserve, and need: and (if it be not our own fault) may get much good by.</ns0:note>] In all this did not Job sin [with his Lips. <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">By any Reflecti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons upon God, by any impatient or unbecoming Expressions.</ns0:note>]</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11. Now when Job's Three Friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place; [Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite: <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Which were Persons then eminent for Birth and Quality, for Wisdom and Knowledge, and for the Profession of the true Reli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gion, being probably of the posterity of <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> and akin to <ns0:hi>Iob,</ns0:hi> and living in the same Country with him.</ns0:note>] for they had made an appointment together, to come to mourn with him, and to comfort him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12. And [when they lift up their Eyes afar off, <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">To wit, at some convenient distance from him: whom they found sitting upon the ground, either in the open Air, or within his own House.</ns0:note>] and [knew him not, <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">His Countenance being so fearfully changed and disfigured by his Boils.</ns0:note>] they lift up their voice, and wept, and they rent every one his Mantle, and [sprink<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led Dust upon their Heads toward Heaven. <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Either upon the upper part of their Heads, which looks towards Heaven: or cast it up into the Air so as it should fall upon their Heads; as they did <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 22. 23. See <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 7. 6. <ns0:hi>Nehem.</ns0:hi> 9. 1. <ns0:hi>Lam.</ns0:hi> 2. 10.</ns0:note>]</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13. So [they sat down with him upon the ground <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">In the posture of Mourners condoling with him.</ns0:note>] [Seven Days, and Seven Nights, <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Which was the usual time of mourning for the Dead, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 50. 10. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 31. 13. and therefore proper both for <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi>'s Children who were dead, and for <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> himself, who was in a manner dead whilst he li<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved: But we must not fancy that they continued in this place and posture so long together, which no Laws of Religion or Civility re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quired of them, and the necessities of Nature could not bear; but only that they spent a great, or the greatest part of that time in sit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ting with him, and silent Mourning over him. And so such General Expressions are frequently understood<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> as <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 2. 37. and 24. 53. <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 20. 31. Either 1. About any thing. Or rather, 2. About his Afflictions and the causes of them. The Reason of this silence was partly the greatness of their grief for him, and their surprize and astonishment at his Condition<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> partly because they thought it convenient to give him some further time to vent his own Sorrows, and partly because as yet they knew not what to say to him: for though they had ever esteemed him to be a truly wise and godly Man, and came with full purpose to comfort him, yet the prodigi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous greatness of his Miseries, and that Hand and Displeasure of God which they manifestly perceived in them, made them at a stand, and to question <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi>'s Sincerity, so that they could not comfort him as they had intended, and yet were loth to grieve him with those Convictions and Reproofs which they thought he greatly needed. And here they stuck till <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> gave them occasion to speak their Minds.</ns0:note>] and [none spake a word to him:] for they saw that <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> Grief was very great.</ns0:p>
